title: AlphaQubit: neural decoder beats matching decoders on Sycamore data
who: Google DeepMind + Google Quantum AI · Nature
what: Transformer decoder for the surface code. On real experimental data at distance 3 and 5 it made 6% fewer errors than tensor-network decoders and 30% fewer than correlated matching; simulated up to distance 11.
artifact: Decoding of real quantum-processor data (offline, not real-time)
caveat: Not real-time in this version; decoding is one component of error correction. The 6% is the paper's distance-5 result (2.748% vs 2.915% logical error per round against the tensor-network decoder); the 30% against correlated matching is Google's blog figure, which the paper's text does not state (correlated-matching rates appear only in Fig. 3).

title: AlphaQubit 2: real-time neural decoding under 1 µs per cycle on TPUs
who: Google DeepMind + Google Quantum AI · arXiv 2512.07737
what: Near-optimal logical error rates on simulated surface codes to distance 23; colour codes decoded to distance 27, where the paper says the result 'does not match the idealized trend'. A compact variant decodes in under 1 µs per cycle (throughput; latency below 500 µs) up to distance 11 on Trillium TPUs. On recorded Willow data (d = 3, 5, 7) it matches AlphaQubit 1 and beats Libra.
artifact: Offline decoding of Willow data; real-time variant demonstrated on TPUs
caveat: Applied to recorded chip data, not yet in a live Willow experiment. 'Under 1 µs per cycle' is throughput (average time per cycle), not latency, which the paper puts below 500 µs.

title: AlphaEvolve quantum circuits with 10× lower error, run on Willow for molecular simulation
who: Google DeepMind · AlphaEvolve impact report, May 7 2026; experiment: Google Quantum AI et al., arXiv 2510.19550 (v1 22 Oct 2025)
what: The Gemini-driven evolutionary coder evolved a Trotter-circuit generator whose circuits cut the mean approximation error against exact classical simulation from 10.4% to 0.82% within the device's gate budget (the report's '10x lower error'). DeepMind says the circuits enabled molecular simulations on the Willow processor that supported first-of-a-kind experimental demonstrations.
artifact: Circuits executed on Google's Willow quantum processor
caveat: Google's own report; the underlying experiment paper is not named in the post. The post links arXiv 2510.19550 (first submitted 22 Oct 2025), where the figure is simulation-approximation error under a gate budget, scored against a classically pre-computed dataset of OTOCs; the preprint is the company's own, with 323 authors.

title: qBraid × AlphaEvolve: fermion-to-qubit encodings reach distance 5 where hand design reached 3
who: qBraid · arXiv 2606.25870
what: AlphaEvolve edited a seed program that builds encodings from a molecule's interaction graph. Reported: 4.2–5× fewer data qubits for the same protection and 3.4–7.9× lower logical error under exact decoding; held-out BeH₂ and H₂O kept distance 5.
artifact: None; evaluated by exhaustive enumeration and exact decoding
caveat: Simulation only; circuit-level fault tolerance listed as next step

title: Language model generates blueprints for quantum-optics experiments, two of them new
who: University of Tübingen (Arlt, Krenn group) · Nature Machine Intelligence (published 19 Feb 2026)
what: A transformer trained on state-to-blueprint pairs writes Python that constructs an experiment for a whole class of target states. Valid rules for 6 of 20 classes (GHZ, W, Bell among them); 4 matched known solutions, 2 were new.
artifact: None; designs checked by simulated fidelity
caveat: Not built in a lab. The model is a 133-million-parameter transformer trained from random initialization on synthetic state–blueprint pairs, not a general-purpose language model; journal publication 19 February 2026 (arXiv June 2024).

title: GPT-5 supplies the key idea for a quantum-complexity bound (QMA amplification)
who: Aaronson, Witteveen · arXiv 2509.21131
what: Black-box QMA amplification cannot beat doubly-exponential completeness error; the model proposed the construction, humans proved it.
caveat: Pure complexity theory

title: Astra: exponential parallel repetition for entangled games, Lean-certified
who: OpenAI GPT-6 Astra · openai/ten-proofs
what: One of ten Lean-certified results released Aug 1 2026; extends the parallel-repetition guarantee to players sharing entanglement.
caveat: Quantum information theory, no hardware

title: Claude improves on the best published quantum circuits for eight primitives, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more
who: Anthropic (Gu, Kemeny) with Yelin and Lukin (Harvard, QuEra) · post of 16 Oct 2026; paper arXiv 2610.22367
what: Claude Mythos 5 proposed circuits in Python in a closed loop with an evaluator that checks each one and scores it by qubits times gates, with no human input between rounds. Elliptic-curve point addition for the discrete-log problem: after 53 hours, one design uses 12% more qubits but 17× fewer gates than the smallest previous one. The decoder step of Decoded Quantum Interferometry: 12× fewer gates than Google's construction. A storage scheme keeps 19 qubits in reserve where the worst case would take 665, failing about one run in 10,000.
artifact: None; checked by classical simulation (403 million sample decodings for the decoder) and Lean proofs for the modular-inversion design
caveat: Nothing ran on quantum hardware; the gains are gate and qubit counts for machines that do not exist yet. The post says circuit design is only one part of a useful quantum computer and does not address error correction or hardware control. For point addition the post also says people gave a one-paragraph brief and occasional prompts to think more broadly. Company post and company preprint, one group, no independent check yet; the figures here are from the post. The paper (arXiv 2610.22367, 15 Oct 2026) puts the result as seven of the eight tasks cutting both Toffoli and qubit counts against the state of the art, the eighth being a new architecture for modular inversion. It names the search as OpenEvolve with Claude Mythos 5, from a fixed hand-written specification per task, and gives the storage figure as one stack entry of 19 qubits against 665 in the worst case, with more needed with probability 1.0×10⁻⁴. The 17× and 12× figures are the post's wording.

title: Neural decoders trained on an emulator match conventional decoders on a distance-7 colour code run on Quantinuum's Helios
who: Quantinuum (Lavasani and 22 others) · arXiv 2610.24077, 16 Oct 2026; announced 19 Oct 2026
what: Triangular colour codes at distances 3, 5 and 7 on the Helios trapped-ion processor reached logical error rates as low as 5×10⁻⁶, with errors suppressed by a factor Λ = 12 for each step in distance (Tesseract decoder). A convolutional network and a transformer, trained on emulator data and applied to the hardware data without fine-tuning, reached 'comparable logical performance', with Λ of 7 and 8, at 0.22 to 0.52 ms of GPU time per round.
artifact: Offline decoding of data recorded on the Helios processor
caveat: The headline figures are those of Tesseract, a conventional search decoder that the paper says is 'generally not fast enough to be used in real time'; the neural decoders are offered as a route to real-time decoding and scale less well (Λ of 7 and 8 against 12). The paper states that 'all decoding in this work has been done offline'. The networks were trained on emulator data only, and the paper notes the emulator may miss error channels on the device. Quantinuum's post gives the distance-7 statistics as 3 failures in 29,000 shots of 20 rounds. Company preprint; a memory experiment, not a computation.

title: Gemini 4 agents write quantum programs with machine-checked proofs of correctness and cost, up to 290× cheaper than prior baselines
who: Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI (Shirobokov, Jaderberg, … Babbush, Chaudhuri, Kohli; 25 authors) · arXiv 2611.09822, 6 Nov 2026 (v3 16 Nov)
what: Teams of Gemini 4 agents write quantum programs in a Lean library against formal specifications and prove their correctness and cost. Reported against the strongest prior baselines: up to 2.57× fewer expected oracle rounds for parallel Grover search, a 290× spacetime reduction for fixed-point arcsin (3,698 T gates on 100 qubits), and 11.8×, 8.22× and 2.49× reductions for simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug metabolism.
artifact: None; programs verified by formal proof in Lean
caveat: Resource counts for fault-tolerant machines that do not exist yet; nothing ran on hardware, and the abstract's own point is that these are algorithms 'that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test'. The proofs certify that each program meets its formal specification, and the paper says researchers 'choose the problems and carefully prepare faithful formal specifications'. The 290× figure combines a classical search with the formal one. Company preprint, no independent check yet.

title: Claude finds a key-recovery attack on HAWK; the scheme is withdrawn from NIST's post-quantum process
who: Anthropic (Weis), confirmed by Apon · NIST pqc-forum, July 28 2026
what: Reduces HAWK-n to SVP in dimension n/2+1; HAWK-512 security from 2^150 to 2^108; a HAWK-256 key recovered in hours. HAWK team withdrew the next day.
artifact: None physical; a real-world standards consequence
caveat: Not physics; included because it is the clearest case of an LLM changing something outside a paper

title: Riemann Hypothesis: a Lean proof by Levent Alpöge working with Claude, certified correct by the Lean and Mathlib communities
who: Levent Alpöge (Anthropic) with Claude · note and Lean library at alpo.ge, 20 Nov 2026; joint statement of the Lean and Mathlib communities, 21 Nov 2026
what: A four-page note says 'I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis', released only as a Lean library of about 17 million lines. The author writes that he guided the approach and that 'Claude far outpaced me near the finish line'. The next day the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative, wrote 'We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct': the theorem proved is exactly Mathlib's statement, and the exported proof passed Lean's kernel and several independent checkers.
caveat: Not physics or engineering; included for its weight, as a Millennium Prize problem. A formal proof only: the note says 'I decided to only present Lean', there is no written proof for people to read, and nothing has been refereed. The author writes that he is 'presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics'. The certification speaks of the Riemann Hypothesis as stated in Mathlib; it does not mention the generalized hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, which the note also claims and the library also states. The Clay Mathematics Institute had posted nothing about it as of 23 Nov 2026. The author is an Anthropic employee according to coverage, Anthropic makes Claude, and the note does not say which Claude model was used. Update, 26 Nov 2026: the note is unchanged, no written proof has been posted and Clay's site still shows nothing. The author's own page at alpo.ge lists Anthropic, so his employer no longer rests on coverage.

title: GNoME predicts 2.2 million crystals; 736 match later experimental entries; A-Lab synthesizes 36 of 57 targets (corrected from 41 of 58)
who: Google DeepMind, LBNL A-Lab · Nature
what: Graph-network screening found 381,000 predicted-stable structures; the 736 'independently realized' structures are matches between GNoME predictions and entries that reached the ICSD after the March 2021 snapshot, not prospective tests. Berkeley's autonomous lab made 36 of 57 chosen targets in 17 days (41 of 58 as first published; corrected 19 January 2026).
caveat: Cheetham & Seshadri (Chem. Mater. 2024) found few new or useful materials among the predictions, mostly compositional variants; Palgrave questioned several A-Lab syntheses. Nature author correction of 19 Jan 2026 (Nature 650, E1, to the A-Lab paper 10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w): 'novel' meant new to the prediction platform, not necessarily new to science; a post-publication re-analysis confirmed 36 of the 40 reported successes, four being inconclusive by XRD, and one compound (Zn2Cr3FeO8) was removed as mistakenly included in the training data. GNoME paper: 10.1038/s41586-023-06735-9.

title: Microsoft + PNNL screen 32 million candidates to 18 and synthesize a sodium-lithium solid electrolyte
who: Microsoft Azure Quantum Elements, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory · J. Am. Chem. Soc. 146, 20009 (2024)
what: AI screening plus HPC filtering produced a candidate electrolyte that was synthesized and tested in a prototype cell within months.
caveat: Company-reported; a candidate, not a product. Peer-reviewed later: Chen et al., J. Am. Chem. Soc. 146(29), 20009–20018, published 9 July 2024 (10.1021/jacs.4c03849); the January 2024 announcement predates the paper.

title: MatterGen designs TaCr₂O₆; synthesized with bulk modulus within 20% of target
who: Microsoft Research, SIAT Shenzhen · Nature
what: A diffusion model generated a structure for a target bulk modulus of 200 GPa; the synthesized (disordered) compound's bulk modulus was estimated at up to 169 GPa, the maximum of four nanoindentation measurements (158 ± 11 GPa) of Young's modulus converted with a DFT-computed Poisson ratio of 0.30.
caveat: One demonstration compound. The 169 GPa is inferred, not measured directly: Young's modulus by nanoindentation, a DFT Poisson ratio, and the maximum of four readings taken because the powder sample is 'likely non-compact'. Juelsholt (Materials Horizons 13, 5672, 2026; ChemRxiv preprint June 2025) argues the disordered product is the known Ta1/2Cr1/2O2 phase, reported in 1971 (1972 in the preprint's abstract) and present in MatterGen's training data.

title: AlphaEvolve: a circuit design fabricated into a TPU; ~4× faster ML force fields at Schrödinger; multi-fold lithography speedups at Substrate
who: Google DeepMind · AlphaEvolve impact report, May 7 2026
what: The Gemini-driven system is a standing tool in next-generation TPU design and one of its circuits is in silicon. Partners report ~4× speedups in training and inference of machine-learned force fields and multi-fold runtime gains in computational lithography.
artifact: Silicon; faster simulation pipelines for chemistry and chip manufacturing
caveat: Partner-reported figures; no new material or compound named

title: Lila Sciences' AI-run lab synthesizes 2,942 catalysts and finds palladium families for green-hydrogen electrolysis
who: Lila Sciences · arXiv 2609.30133, Sept 24 2026
what: An in-house proposer combining Bayesian methods with language models chose each cycle's compositions; automated PVD synthesis, screening and characterization. Six palladium-oxide families near the activity–stability frontier; InMnPdOₓ stayed below 0.5 V overpotential for over 1,000 hours in 1 M sulfuric acid.
caveat: Company preprint; 'comparable to ruthenium' is their comparison, no benchmark numbers given; humans still moved samples. The preprint (arXiv 2609.30133) does give benchmark numbers, all against films made on the same platform: InMnPdOx held 0.45 V overpotential at 10 mA/cm², within 40 mV of their RuOx (0.41 V); PdOx passed 0.5 V at about 200 h and NiTaPdOx at about 470 h. It calls the platform human-supervised with over 90% automation; operators move sample fixtures and start instruments.

title: LLM recipe generator guides the first synthesis of three unreported oxy-selenides, with people running the experiments
who: Jeon, Kim, … Li, Cho (Sungkyunkwan University, Ajou University, KICET, MIT) · Advanced Materials 38, e74502
what: A retrieval-augmented language model built on recipes extracted from 4,407 papers proposed solid-state routes for DFT-screened solid-electrolyte candidates. Fed back XRD results, it brought LiCr(SeO₃)₂ to single phase at 400 °C, then LiAl(SeO₃)₂ and CsLiSeO₄ in three guided experiments each, and found a new route to the known LiGa(SeO₃)₂.
caveat: Humans chose the targets by first-principles screening and did every synthesis step (mortar, tube furnace, XRD) themselves; the model's claimed contribution is fewer trial-and-error cycles. Three new compounds from one group, published 10 Aug 2026, no independent replication yet

title: ElementsClaw: an agent built on language models and an atomic model guides the synthesis of four new superconductors, with transition temperatures of 2.5 to 6.5 K
who: Alibaba DAMO Academy, Renmin University of China and others (Li, Rong and 17 others) · arXiv 2604.23758, 26 Apr 2026 (v3 4 May 2026)
what: The agent combines language models (GPT-5 for reading the literature) with a 1-billion-parameter atomic model. It screened 2.4 million crystals to 68,000 superconductor candidates in 28 GPU hours and rediscovered 66 known superconductors missing from the standard database. Four of its picks were synthesized and confirmed by X-ray diffraction and by magnetic or transport measurements: Zr₃ScRe₈ (6.5 K), HfZrRe₄ (5.9 K), Zr₄VRe₇ (3.5 K) and Hf₂₁Re₂₅ (2.5 K).
artifact: Synthesized intermetallic compounds with measured superconducting transitions
caveat: One group's preprint, with no independent synthesis yet. The paper says the agent was 'guided by human expertise' and that its literature judgments were sorted 'after manual verification'; the authors selected which candidates to make and made them. The highest transition temperature is 6.5 K. Hf₂₁Re₂₅ was already in the structure databases (the paper calls it 'database-latent') and Zr₄VRe₇ was a predicted entry in the GNoME dataset with a different structure; what is new for those two is the superconductivity and the structure. The paper's own figures vary: Hf₂₁Re₂₅ is 2.5 K in the abstract, with onset at 3.0 K and zero resistance at 2.0 K in the text.

title: Machine-learning screen predicts kagome superconductors; YRu₃B₂ and LuRu₃B₂ are made and superconduct below 1 K
who: Albu Mustaf, … Törmä, Marques, Bernevig, Morosan (Rice, Aalto, Bochum, Princeton, DIPC) · Physical Review Research 8, 023308 (17 June 2026)
what: A machine-learning-accelerated high-throughput screen of the 1:3:2 kagome family, combined with first-principles calculations, predicted several stable superconductors. Arc-melted samples of YRu₃B₂ and LuRu₃B₂ showed bulk superconductivity at 0.81 K and 0.95 K, confirmed by magnetization, specific heat and electrical transport, with superconducting volume fractions close to 100%.
artifact: Synthesized compounds with measured superconducting transitions
caveat: Only YRu₃B₂ came out of the screen: the paper says LuRu₃B₂ 'was initially overlooked in our high-throughput predictions' because its calculated phonon spectrum had weakly imaginary modes. Both transitions are below 1 K. The screen is a conventional machine-learning model, not a language model, and was reported in an earlier paper by the same group. arXiv 2512.16945 is the preprint.

title: Claude designs three electronic devices from short prompts; the boards are manufactured from its files and work without fixes to their circuitry
who: Anthropic with Diode Computers · anthropic.com, 9 Nov 2026
what: Claude Fable 5.2 produced the schematics, board layouts, enclosures, firmware and parts lists for a USB speakerphone, a voice-assistant hub and a handheld virtual pet, and ran the manufacturing and sourcing checks itself. The post says Diode 'manufactured all three boards directly from Claude's design files, without any back-and-forth over adjustments', and that the prototypes 'worked without any fixes to their circuitry'.
caveat: A company post about its own model, and 'Anthropic has a commercial relationship with Diode'. Three one-off prototypes of ordinary consumer devices: the post says 'they haven't been through electrical validation, antenna tuning, thermal testing, or certification' and 'weren't designed for mass production'. Engineers at Diode assembled and tested the boards, since Claude 'wasn't connected to test equipment or to the machines that make and assemble circuit boards', and gave it short prompts along the way. No paper or data release.

title: Reinforcement learning controls the plasma in a tokamak
who: Google DeepMind + EPFL Swiss Plasma Center · Nature
what: A single RL controller shaped and held plasma configurations in the TCV tokamak, including shapes not previously produced there.
artifact: Live control of a fusion experiment
caveat: A control-engineering result, not new plasma physics

title: GraphCast beats ECMWF's operational forecast on 90% of targets; GenCast beats the ensemble on 97%
who: Google DeepMind · Science (2023), Nature (2024)
what: Learned weather models outperform the leading physics-based system at 10-day forecasts; ECMWF now runs its own learned model operationally.
artifact: Operational forecasts used by weather services
caveat: Prediction, not explanation; trained on physics-model reanalysis

title: Physics-tailored neural network reveals unexpected non-reciprocal forces in dusty plasma, confirmed by experiment
who: Emory University (Burton, Nemenman) · PNAS 122(31)
what: A custom physics-structured network trained on 3D particle tracks described non-reciprocal interparticle forces with >99% accuracy and showed two textbook assumptions (charge–size relation, screening-length dependence) are wrong; follow-up experiments confirmed it.
caveat: Small system; custom architecture, not a general model

title: Unstable self-similar singularities found in fluid equations with physics-informed neural networks
who: Google DeepMind, Brown, NYU, Stanford · arXiv 2509.14185
what: New families of unstable blow-up profiles for incompressible porous media and 3D Euler with boundary, to near machine precision.
caveat: Framed as groundwork for Navier–Stokes; experts note real fluids have no singularity

title: GPT-5 science paper: black-hole symmetries, cosmic-string gravitational-wave spectra, thermonuclear burn modeling
who: OpenAI with Lupsasca, Scherrer, Spears (LLNL) · arXiv 2511.16072
what: Case studies where GPT-5 contributed derivations or reduced-physics models; the burn-propagation case produced a working ridge-map code for inertial-confinement fusion modeling.
caveat: Company-curated case studies; mixed novelty

title: GPT-5.2 Pro proposes a new gluon scattering-amplitude formula; OpenAI model proves it
who: Guevara (IAS), Lupsasca, Skinner, Strominger, Weil · arXiv 2602.12176
what: For one negative-helicity gluon the tree amplitude, assumed zero, is nonzero on a special slice of momentum space; the model proposed the closed form after humans computed cases to n = 6. Arkani-Hamed and Craig commented favorably.
caveat: Preprint; no experimental consequence claimed

title: Claude computes the nine-loop six-point amplitude in planar N=4 super Yang–Mills
who: Anthropic (Fitzpatrick, Mishra-Sharma), checked by Dixon; von Hippel's public challenge
what: Previous record was eight loops (2023). Two internal representations agreed on all 107,053 nonzero coefficients at symbol level (the beyond-symbol completion was computed once, with no second independent computation); the bootstrap took about $100 of CPU (96 CPUs for a week), and von Hippel puts either approach at one to two thousand dollars once Claude's time is counted.
caveat: A record computation in a toy model, by known methods; von Hippel says it did not produce the new methods he hoped for

title: Navier–Stokes finite-time singularity under smooth forcing (Clay statements C and D), Lean-formalized
who: OpenAI internal model, ~10,000 agents · Sept 8 2026
what: Blow-up from a smooth fluid at rest under a smooth external force. Clay called the problem 'apparently settled' (Sept 11) with review ongoing; OpenAI is not claiming the prize.
caveat: Unforced case still open. Bastounis–Circelli–Hansen (arXiv 2610.08144) show the Lean code and the 166-page paper are not the same proof (a Lean lemma needs m+5 derivatives where the paper claims m+4) while explicitly not claiming either is wrong. Says where the continuum model breaks, nothing about real fluids. Hales (guest post on Tao's blog, 9 Oct 2026) reports the Lean formalisation 'has already been confirmed by more than a dozen proof-checkers'; the open question is whether the Lean statement is the paper's theorem, not whether the Lean proof checks. Update, 26 Nov 2026: 'Unforced case still open' no longer describes the claims on record. On 20 Nov 2026 Alpöge and Buckmaster posted a claimed proof of blow-up without force (item P14), whose central certificate is not yet released. Clay's site shows nothing newer than its statement of 11 September.

title: OpenAI's 372-family release: 70 families in PDE, mathematical physics, quantum information and statistical physics
who: OpenAI unreleased internal model · github.com/openai/math, Oct 6 2026
what: Includes universal computation in forced Navier–Stokes, De Giorgi in dimension 8, a uniform Hilbert's 16th bound, Parity ∉ QAC⁰. About 42% (300 of 719) of top-line results Lean-formalised; 3 manuscripts withdrawn Oct 7 (722 to 719). On 26 Oct 2026 two manuscripts with Lean formalisations were added, Sogge's local smoothing conjecture in every dimension at least two (the repository says it also yields the Kakeya conjectures) and a refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, taking the catalogue to 721 manuscripts in 373 families. On 23 and 24 Nov 2026 ten more manuscripts were added: 'VP and VNP are different', seven on tensor geometry, one of them titled 'The matrix multiplication exponent is nine fourths', and two on linear programming, one of which says it answers Smale's ninth problem. The README now gives 730 manuscripts in 375 families.
caveat: Mostly unreviewed; no human has yet read most of them. The 70 is the catalogue's own sections Mathematical physics (25, which hold the quantum-information families), Partial differential equations (16) and Probability and statistical mechanics (29). 'No human has read most of them' is the author's inference: the repository says the manuscripts came from a fixed model-driven procedure, that some unformalised results 'could have issues', and that one writeup was human-edited; it does not say who has read them. The 26 Oct history entry says a working group led by Impagliazzo, Paturi and Williams 'will examine and explain' the ETH proof and that the materials were made public at the group's request; the README still puts the formalised share at '~42%'. The November additions are complexity theory and combinatorics, outside the 70 families counted here, and the history entry says they come with Lean formalisations 'of selected results from each manuscript'.

title: OpenAI model's Lean proof constructs four-dimensional Yang–Mills theory, in its review group's judgment; no uniqueness, no mass gap, and the QCD part is not public
who: OpenAI unnamed internal model · announced 26 Oct 2026; Lean sources, assessment of 10 Nov 2026 and summary of 25 Nov 2026 by the Yang–Mills group (prepared by Douglas, Jaffe, Nissim and Rajasekaran; led by David Gross, per OpenAI's announcement as reported) · github.com/yang-mills-group
what: OpenAI submitted Lean code on 27 Oct 2026 (the archive is dated 28 Oct). The reviewing group's assessment of 10 Nov says that in its judgment the submission proves that 'a relativistic quantum field theory satisfying the Wightman axioms can be constructed as a scaling limit of four-dimensional Wilson lattice gauge theory for any simple compact gauge group'. A clean rebuild, an axiom audit and a Comparator check passed, and the group added Lean checks of its own. OpenAI's announcement, as reported, also covered theories with fermions, QCD among them; the assessment covers pure Yang–Mills only. A second submission of 4 Nov adds matching to a perturbative reference at every finite order; the group's summary of 25 Nov says agreement of that reference with conventional Yang–Mills perturbation theory 'remains under review'.
caveat: Nothing is public: no paper, no Lean code, no model named. Coverage says the model produced a Yang–Mills existence proof on 9 Sept and a QCD proof on 18 Sept and that the Yang–Mills formalisation was finished on 16 Oct; none of it is released. No mass gap is claimed, so it is not the Clay problem. A mathematical existence proof for a theory physicists have computed with for fifty years says nothing about any experiment. Update, 10 Nov 2026: part of this changed. The Lean sources for the pure Yang–Mills part are now public and assessed (github.com/yang-mills-group). The assessment says the submission 'does not prove that the infinite-volume limit is unique or that there is a mass gap', that it 'does not draw on the separate informal proof manuscript', and 'We do not claim to fully understand the proof yet'; the group used OpenAI's Astra model to digest the Lean code. It lists a second OpenAI submission (4 Nov) and one from Alpöge and Sussman (15 Nov) as work in progress. The QCD claim still has no public proof or assessment, and coverage says the written proof is unreleased. Update, 25 Nov 2026: the group's summary of OpenAI's second submission (4 Nov) says 'human review so far is limited' and 'Neither release establishes a mass gap or a unique infinite-volume limit'; its supporting reports are AI-generated first drafts. The Alpöge and Sussman submission is still listed as work in progress. The group now dates the first submission 27 Oct, the day it received the files.

title: Machine-learning controllers run heating and current drive in five experiments on the DIII-D tokamak, one of them fully under a reinforcement-learning model
who: Princeton University, Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, QST (Rothstein, Farre-Kaga, … Kolemen) · Nuclear Fusion 66, 076050 (online 2 July 2026)
what: PACMAN is a framework that takes diagnostics in and sends actuator commands out. The paper describes five experiments on DIII-D that used it: a reinforcement-learning controller for advanced non-inductive plasmas, an ELM predictor, an Alfvén-eigenmode controller, a model-predictive profile controller and a tearing-mode predictor-controller. In the reinforcement-learning case the model's outputs 'fully decide actuator commands', within hard-coded safety limits, on a 50 ms cycle (shot 204975).
artifact: Live control of a fusion experiment
caveat: A control-system paper: it describes the framework and shows example discharges, and does not show that the experiments could not have been run with conventional controllers. The reinforcement-learning controller was trained offline in a simulator. The quotations are from the preprint, arXiv 2511.08818 (11 Nov 2025); the date here is the journal's.

title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes: a calculation set up in 2003 and an exact bootstrap bound
who: Anthropic (Hongbin Chen) · anthropic.com, 17 Nov 2026; two preprints linked from the post
what: Agents working for about six weeks on 22 open problems that Claude had listed solved two. One completed a calculation that physicists set out in 2003 and showed that the phase transition tied to black-hole formation is abrupt even where spacetime has no definite shape; a physicist working separately with Claude reached the same answer by a different method. The other found the exact ceiling given by the simplest version of the modular bootstrap and proved it cannot be lowered; the post says those results were formally verified in Lean and that a physicist checked every main result.
caveat: Theory about simplified model universes: the post says 'Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications', and that neither 'settles the question of quantum gravity, or even comes close'. A company post about its own model. One half of the bootstrap proof 'follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof' of a sphere-packing result. The two preprints are hosted at hexagonmath.org and were not opened for this entry.

title: Finite-time blow-up for the three-dimensional Euler equations without force, from smooth periodic data; LLM-assisted and Lean-formalized
who: Alpöge, Buckmaster, Coiculescu · arXiv 2611.26772, 19 Nov 2026; Lean formalization at github.com/mcoiculescu/EulerBlowupPublic
what: The paper constructs smooth periodic initial data for the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations whose solution blows up in finite time with no external force: the velocity stays bounded while the vorticity at the origin tends to infinity. Its AI statement says 'We used Claude and Codex throughout this work' and that 'The first proof without force was written by Anthropic models' from the authors' earlier drafts. The repository holds a Lean formalization in one-to-one correspondence with the paper's proof, with no sorry and only the three standard axioms.
caveat: Mathematics of an idealized fluid with no viscosity; it says nothing about a real fluid. A preprint one week old, formalized by its own authors and not refereed; the repository lists exceptions to the correspondence, among them a criterion cited by one corollary that is not formalized. The authors rewrote the models' first proof 'under our direction' and 'replaced parts of the argument by ideas of our own'. The paper says OpenAI had already released a paper on the unforced Euler equations built on the same amplification mechanism, and gives the authors' account of priority; OpenAI's paper was not opened for this entry.

title: Alpöge and Buckmaster claim finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations without force, with Claude; the certificate the proof rests on is not yet released
who: Alpöge and Buckmaster · paper of 20 Nov 2026 and Lean package at github.com/tristanbuckmaster/navier-stokes
what: The abstract claims smooth, compactly supported initial data on R³, and smooth data on the torus, for which solutions of the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations without force blow up in finite time, which it says 'disproves the statements (A) and (B) of the Millennium Prize problem as formulated by Fefferman, and hence proves the statements (C) and (D)'. The blow-up profile is obtained from a certificate, an approximate solution satisfying explicit inequalities, verified by interval arithmetic. The AI statement reads 'We used Anthropic models (Claude) throughout this work, and no others.'
caveat: Not yet checkable. The paper says 'The certificate will be released soon' and gives only its hash. The repository says 'The formalization contains no data', that the interval-arithmetic computation verifying the certificate is not part of the formalization and is not in the repository, and that the patched Lean package 'was not rebuilt when this repository was assembled'. Posted on GitHub, not on arXiv, and not refereed; Clay has posted nothing. It is mathematics about the equations, not about a real fluid. OpenAI's result of September (P8) needed an external force; this claim is for the case without one.
